entries.claim: The entry attests absolvo with a heavy penultimate syllable and the distinct senses of freeing, acquitting, and completing. An ironic usage label is not a lexical meaning.
Second-conjugation infinitive requires long-ē penult, as shown by L&S n226 conjugation 2.
The noun includes acts or activity, dramatic performance, a technical right of passage for cattle or carts, and Roman land measures. The land measures have more than one set of dimensions.
The noun includes building or construction and, figuratively, edification or instruction.
Deponent first-conjugation verb with both emulation and envy senses. In caritas non aemulatur, love is the subject of envying, not its passive object.
L&S n1460, XML line 1813: af-fĕro, attŭli, allātum, afferre. Infinitive penult is closed; allātum has long ā.
The entry documents the intransitive sense of appearing or showing oneself; it does not supply prayer-translation wording.
Standard third-conjugation transitive verb, attested for hanging and weighing. The rarer appendeo variant is genuine. This lexical identity does not alone decide the poetic image in Proverbs 8:29.
The attention and application-of-mind sense supports the command to pay heed.
The noun denotes a state of happiness or blessedness, not an act of blessing.
The noun calamus denotes a reed and, by metonymy, a reed pen. It is the nominative predicate in lingua mea calamus scribae, not a first-person verb.
Includes instruments sounding as well as singing, with tubae among the cited instrument subjects.

The sole current occurrence is dico ego carmen meum Regi after effundit cor meum verbum bonum: an uttered song/poem addressed to the King, not a textile card. L&S carmen1 explicitly covers song, poem and dicere carmen. carmen2 is a genuine different homograph but has no consumer here.
The ordinary chair or seat sense precedes specialized teaching and ecclesiastical uses.
The noun includes heedfulness, security or a guarantee, and an obligation or bond, written as well as oral.

Matthias is joined to the apostolic college/company, not enrolled in a school. College itself is valid and is retained; the current college, school equivalence unnecessarily restricts the social/body-of-colleagues sense and misleads in this context.
The noun denotes a column, pillar or post, also figurative support and a waterspout; the entry explicitly includes a pillar of cloud.

The entry distinguishes trade from wider exchange, intercourse and fellowship. These senses support the sacred-exchange context; the dictionary is lexical evidence, not a source of either prayer translation.

locator.section: Perseus TEI entry n9532 and n9533

entries.claim: The dictionary distinguishes comparison or matching from preparation or procurement in two entries with the same principal parts; both ranges are represented under the shared lemma.
The verb includes bringing together, winning favor or commending, and obtaining or procuring, not only arranging a marriage.
The ordinary senses include an assembly or council, an association or company, and union or bond.
The verb includes enclosing or confining, as well as finishing, composing a sentence, and reasoning to a conclusion.
The verb includes bringing together, heaping up, building and compiling. The separate noun entry is not its lexical identity.
The deponent entry supplies principal parts and both follow and attain or obtain senses; the collect selects the latter sense.
The verb includes standing or taking position, halting, remaining or existing, and depending on or consisting in something.
The substantive includes a sharer, partner, or companion, without restricting the company to women.
The verb includes placing, establishing, appointing and determining, including appointment of a person to a position.

The noun includes constitution, disposition, order and arrangement and is derived from constituo. Establishment in the phrase about the world is a contextual derivational rendering, not a quoted English gloss in this entry.

Omnia in ipso constant has omnia as plural subject: all created things hold together/subsist in Christ. The impersonal it-is-agreed family is legitimate elsewhere but does not explain this actual clause. Full consto covers standing together/firmly, existence and constitution/dependence.
The ordinary senses include custom, habit and usage; the entry also distinguishes social familiarity from specifically sexual intercourse.
The feminine noun includes restraint of passions and desires, continence, temperance and moderation. The separate neuter plural cross-reference is not this noun.

The verb includes holding together, retaining, restraining and containing. Closing the ears is a contextual rendering of the enclosure or restraint range, not a verse-specific English quotation from the dictionary.
The verb includes gathering, contraction, incurring consequences or guilt, and making an agreement or relationship; the entry expressly illustrates incurring culpam.
The adjective includes opposite or hostile, with substantival contrary or reverse and the adverbial phrase e contrario.
The entry supports association and frequent use. It is not cited for the later Christian conduct or way-of-life sense, whose evidence is recorded separately.
The full entry includes a wreath or garland and a royal crown, with reward uses.
The verb includes physical destruction or ruin as well as spoiling, moral corruption, bribery and falsification; conrumpo is a spelling variant.

The fourth-declension noun includes worship and veneration, cultivation and care, training and culture, and clothing or adornment. The participle and the neighboring cultivated-lands noun are distinct identities.
The noun includes attentive care, concern or anxiety, administrative charge and medical attendance. Administrative office is not its sole ordinary meaning.
The noun includes healing or medical treatment as well as care, management and administration.
Both occurrences are the repeated nox in suo cursu medium iter haberet: the night's course/passage, not a lesson. Full cursus supports physical and temporal course; no local educational consumer.
The noun primarily includes defending or defense, including an argumentative defense. Specialized legal prosecution is a separate attested branch, not the sole meaning.
The verb includes bringing, offering or conferring something on someone, and reporting. These ordinary senses must not be replaced by rare late senses alone.
The ordinary noun denotes delight, pleasure or enjoyment. The late medical straining sense is separately identified and does not replace that ordinary meaning.
The verb includes literal devouring or swallowing, consuming property, and figurative suppression or patient endurance.
The adjective includes the spatial right-hand sense, explicitly with manus, as well as dexterity, favorable circumstances and suitability; the forms dextera and dextra are both attested.
L&S n13895, XML line 14272: dif-fundo, fūdi, fūsum, 3. The perfect has no nasal; stress follows closed/long penults.
The genitive quantity supports dolóris.
The vowel quantities support dolorósus; the adjective describes experienced sorrow.

The ordinary deponent means to rule or exercise dominion, including inanimate subjects and a dative complement. The separately illustrated passive being-ruled use does not describe death exercising dominion in the Easter clause.

The introductory construction rule and examples allow nominative phrases or clauses and independent accusatives, particularly in early Latin. The noun inside an introduced clause can receive its case from that clause.
The noun entry supports result or effect. The collect selects a beneficial result, expressed idiomatically as fruit, not the unrelated supine analysis.
The entry supports the first-conjugation principal forms and the figurative pouring-forth sense, including Psalm 44:2. The token perfect is not a noun or a present-tense form.
The head ē-vādo, si, sum supplies the long vowel in the principal parts; the entry supports the sense of escaping.
The entry records felicis with long i and favorable or prosperous senses; it supports the head accent and contextual adjective, not a feeling of happiness in this occurrence.

Ficus has mixed second- and fourth-declension forms and attested feminine and masculine gender. The Gospel object ficus parallels accusative plural uvas. The lexical alternatives do not establish every occurrence's case or number.

The adverb is treated under fidelis: faithful or trustworthy action, reliable retention, and secure or firm establishment. The separate ecclesiastical reliance-on-God wording retained on the card is not quoted from this entry.
L&S n18173, XML line 18564: fīlĭa, ae; short penult i in filiae and house æ ligature. Printed tract fíliæ independently confirms the accent.
The second-conjugation infinitive has long e, supporting florére and perfect floruit.
The entry attests the ecclesiastical plural sense referring to pagan peoples alongside the broader senses of race, nation and people; it does not determine every occurrence.
The third-declension noun includes descent, race or people, and kinds or classes. Noble birth is only a narrower use; the separate fourth-declension cross-reference belongs to genu.
The entry explicitly attests a mother as subject, supporting Virgo genuit.
The principal sense is a sword, with attested figurative death or murder and a remote fish sense. The collected scriptural occurrences select sword, not swordfish.
The demonstrative hic, haec, hoc points to a near or present referent. The separately labeled adverbial section does not supply a free-standing here sense for the inflected pronoun.
The indeclinable adverb hic means here, in this place, with extended temporal or situational uses. It is separately identified from the demonstrative in the same dictionary entry.
The noun denotes a blow, stroke or thrust, not a verb meaning to push.
The adjective denotes suitability, capability or sufficiency. Solvency is a specialized application rather than its sole meaning.

L&S n21759 gives immortālĭtas, ātis: genitive stress belongs on tā, not li. The compact senses are restricted to exemption from death and imperishableness. An unqualified equivalent meaning divinity is not supported by this entry.
L&S n21790 gives immūto, āvi, ātum, 1. Long ū in present and long first-conjugation ā in the remaining forms.
The entry redirects to inferus, whose superlatives include imus and infimus. The substantivized neuter plural denotes lower things, not a masculine population.
The accusative temporal subsection attests duration including in aeternum, not only spatial direction.
The adjective includes what cannot be estimated, inestimable or invaluable. The negative philosophical valuation is explicitly separate and does not displace the affirmative sense.
L&S n22579 gives in-corruptĭo, ōnis; genitive stress on ō.
L&S n22582 in-corruptus; closed rup penult determines stress.
Includes putting on clothing and figurative assumption, not only clothing another person.

The entry attests the principal parts inspicio, inspicere, inspexi, inspectum and literal inspection or close looking, with figurative consideration. The selected perfect inspexerunt comes from the controlling liturgical print.

The clause is instantia mea cotidiana, followed by care for all the churches. Daily belongs to the separate adjective cotidiana, not the noun's lexical definition. Preserve pressure, and expose urgency/persistence supported by the full primary entry; no claim that the existing whole phrase daily pressure is a mistranslation.

The entry includes absolute exertion and intention as well as transitive stretching or directing; this does not supply an unexpressed horse, chariot, or command to fight. Directing attention, attentive observation and attentive listening are also explicit branches of the entry.
The noun includes intervention or occurrence and, in transferred use, mediation or assistance. The closed penult determines its stress.

The adjective has nominative invisibilis and neuter invisibile, conventionally displayed invisibilis, -e. It denotes what is invisible or unseen; invisibil is only the retained identifier, not a Latin nominative.
The paradigm is, ea, id includes feminine personal reference as well as masculine and neuter.

Both repeated occurrences are ex ore infantium et lactentium: children/suckling infants praising God, not sacrificial animals. Full lacteo includes human sucklings as well as animals; the current animal-only expansion is misleading. The corpus lexicalized substantival lactens representation is not changed here.
L&S n27919, XML line 28335: mansŭētūdo, ĭnis; long penult tū in nominative.
The substantive meritum can mean a reward or recompense as well as a meritorious deed; these senses are distinct within the prayer.

All seven occurrences in six texts concern service or ministry, including angels, Christian ministers and apostolic office. The state-only restriction is false for these contexts; the complete entry explicitly identifies Christian ministry.

L&S n29521 mōmentum; closed men penult determines stress, regardless of long initial mō. The time-instant sense is directly attested, including in momento, in ictu oculi; the compact card includes that contextual sense.
The first-conjugation verb means to multiply, increase or augment; its long-vowel endings determine the displayed stress.

Both occurrences are the bonds of sins from which petitioners seek release. A creditor/debtor obligation is a genuine secondary legal sense, but the card omits the basic binding/fetter sense needed by both metaphors. The whole nexus2 entry supports literal binding and figurative restraints.

L&S n32775 heads the impersonal oportet, uit, 2. Do not display fabricated first-person opórteo or supine oportúitum. Both analyzers link this form under the existing corpus key, so a key migration is not required for this repair. The construction expresses impersonal necessity or obligation, not a personal command.

All nineteen occurrences in thirteen Gospels concern Jesus' spoken parables, comparisons or figurative teaching. A mathematical curve is not the referent. L&S explicitly gives comparison and ecclesiastical parable; the current technical sense does not cover any reviewed occurrence.
The entry supplies the long-i infinitive and perfect and passing-through sense; the collect uses the perfect figuratively of a sword piercing the soul.

locator.section: Perseus TEI entry n37456, with its explicit cross-reference to n37457 II

entries.claim: The two Joseph prefaces praise God with due praeconiis, and the Innocents proclaim His praise by dying. The full praeconium cross-reference was followed to praeconius II: proclamation and laudation are supported; commercial advertisement alone is misleading.
The entry records prophecy or prediction and long i in prophetia; it supports the corrected principal form and prophetic sense.
The adverb prospere is explicitly attested, including its combination with procedere; it is not the vocative adjective in this exhortation.
The entry refers to propior, including the superlative and substantive senses of close companions or neighbors.
The dictionary marks the long nominative penult of pulchritudo, supporting pulchritúdo.
The second-conjugation verb includes recounting or going over something in thought, besides enumerating or reviewing.
The entry supports the full principal parts and remembering or celebrating sense; the contextual present is recolimus.
The attested accusative-plus-dative construction supports ima summis as object and counterpart.
Restoration is attested alongside returning or rendering, supporting pacem reddidit.

The one occurrence implebuntur horrea tua saturitate concerns barns filled with abundance, not color saturation. The complete entry expressly cites Prov.3:10 under fullness/plenty/abundance. Color depth is genuinely attested but is not a suitable sole sense for this card's consumer.
Includes a single expression, saying or word, not only an extended discourse.
The transferred use introduces enquiry or doubt, including after seeing or considering; ordinary conditional uses remain distinct.
The noun includes a cast lot, an allotted share or duty, and one's portion, condition or destiny. These are distinct attested uses, not interchangeable contextual translations.

The entry explicitly attests beauty as well as appearance; the Eucharistic sense remains separately context-qualified. The aesthetic subsection also attests splendor, within the same related semantic range.
The word includes the human spirit, soul or mind as well as breath and the personal use in Spiritus Sanctus.
The feminine noun sponsa is cross-referenced to spondeo and supplies the bride addressed here.
The literal goad and figurative sting support the biblical metaphor as well as transferred incentive uses.
The entry redirects to superus and its superlative. The substantivized neuter dative plural summis is the counterpart of ima in the construction with reconcilio.
The first-conjugation verb has long-vowel endings in its infinitive, perfect and supine, determining the displayed stress.

All ten occurrences in eight texts concern personal witnesses, including Christ, God, angels, resurrection witnesses and false witnesses. Full testis1 supports witness; testis2 is a genuine anatomical homograph with no local consumer. No anatomical sense is needed in the context-oriented card.
The entry includes literal passage across or along a route as well as passing away and omission.
Second-declension masculine noun denoting a thorn-bearing plant or a caltrop, distinct from third-declension tribulis, a fellow tribesman.
L&S n49341 tŭba, ae. House orthography leaves the two-syllable genitive unaccented and uses æ.
The direct-question use is an interrogative adverb (I.B). Conjunctive uses remain available separately.
The entry identifies the deponent verb and an attested active collateral form. Venerando in the collect is an active-form ablative gerund, not a passive obligation.
The adverb section includes transferred adversative and transitional uses, not only affirmative ones.
L&S n50867 victōrĭa, ae: genitive i is short before the diphthong; stress remains on to; use æ.
The entry supports botanical shoot and rod senses; the two-syllable genitive virgae needs no acute accent.
